passage:
Paragraph A
On the morning of the school art exhibition, Mariam opened a wooden box that her grandfather had kept in a cupboard for years. Inside were faded photographs, two small brushes and a landscape painting of a harbour. She was hesitant to touch the canvas because the paint looked fragile. Her aunt told her that Grandfather had created the picture when he was young. Mariam liked the idea of displaying something made by her family, so she carried it to the library where the exhibition was being prepared. The organiser offered a place near the entrance.

Paragraph B
Mariam wrote a label describing the painting as her grandfather's earliest masterpiece. Then she telephoned him to confirm the title. He sounded surprised. He explained that he had bought the picture from a market stall many years earlier and had never claimed to be its painter. Her aunt had remembered the story incorrectly. Mariam felt embarrassed because her label was already printed, and the doors would open in less than an hour. Some classmates suggested removing the name quietly and keeping the rest of the description. But Mariam wanted visitors to receive accurate information.

Paragraph C
The school librarian offered to help with a meticulous investigation. Together they examined the frame without touching the painting itself. On the back they found an old postcard with a handwritten date, 1978, and a few letters that might have been an artist's initials. The librarian explained that a date and an incomplete signature could not establish who had painted the scene. They photographed the evidence, wrote down what Grandfather could remember, and asked the art teacher to check whether the paint needed special handling. No one was allowed to make a dramatic claim from uncertain clues.

Paragraph D
The organiser asked Mariam to decide what should happen before the opening. Mariam could remove the landscape entirely, but she believed its story might still teach students something important about art. She replaced the original label with a new one saying, Artist not confirmed. Underneath, she explained how the picture came into the family's possession and why the postcard did not prove its creator's identity. Her friends helped adjust the display so visitors could read the new account comfortably. The painting remained beside the entrance, but the misleading attribution disappeared.

Paragraph E
That afternoon an elderly visitor stopped to look at the painting. She recognised a detail in the harbour and remembered seeing a similar picture in a small shop decades earlier. She could not name the artist, but she offered to write down her memory and contact the organiser if she found an old photograph. Mariam felt relieved. The visitor had not solved the mystery, yet she had shown why honesty encourages people to share useful information. At the end of the exhibition, Mariam placed the postcard and every visitor note in a labelled folder, ready for future research.
